This method constructs a half-resolution volumetric representation from a full-resolution input to reduce data size while preserving visual quality and avoiding the information loss associated with direct subsampling [S1].

The claim states that the method constructs a half-resolution volumetric representation from a full-resolution input to reduce data size while preserving visual quality and avoiding information loss associated with direct subsampling. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly describes a 'Pre-processing for Half Resolution' step where a half-resolution volume is created from a full-resolution volume. It details the specific voxel selection and replacement logic (using median of adjacent voxels) to handle transparency and avoid occlusion. Furthermore, the evidence provides quantitative proof that this method avoids the 'significant information loss' of direct subsampling by achieving a higher PSNR (32.08 dB) compared to direct subsampling (22.75 dB), thereby preserving visual quality.

It operates directly in the spatial domain using a specific odd-index subsampling pattern and local median replacement to fill transparent regions [S1].

The claim states that the method operates in the spatial domain using an odd-index subsampling pattern and local median replacement for transparent regions. The evidence confirms: 1) The subsampling pattern uses indices $(2i-1, 2j-1, 2k-1)$, which are odd indices. 2) For transparent voxels in the half-resolution volume, the method checks adjacent full-resolution voxels and replaces the transparent voxel with the median of those adjacent voxels if any are non-transparent. 3) The process describes manipulating voxel locations and values directly, which constitutes operation in the spatial domain.
supported
- **Boundary Conditions:** The subsampling formula $2\hat{i}-1$ ensures odd indices are selected [S1].

The claim states that the subsampling formula $2i-1$ ensures odd indices are selected. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines the inclusion of voxels at locations $(2i-1, 2j-1, 2k-1)$ where $i, j, k$ are integers starting from 1. Mathematically, for any integer $n$, $2n-1$ yields an odd number. Since the indices $i, j, k$ are integers ($1, 2, 3, ...$), the resulting indices $2i-1, 2j-1, 2k-1$ are always odd. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that this formula selects odd indices.
